summary: Adds the INFO method to the Session Initiation Protocol, to carry session-related control information generated during a session. It was later replaced by RFC 6086.

plainLanguage.summary: During a call, you may need to pass little extra messages like button presses. This adds a way to do that.

subtitle: A way for SIP calls to exchange mid-call control information.

tldr.problem: SIP handles call setup and teardown, but once a call is established, there is no standard way to send session-related control information like DTMF tones or signaling between gateways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2976 adds the INFO method, which lets SIP endpoints send optional information along the established call signaling path without changing the call state.
tldr.outcome: INFO provides a general-purpose mechanism for mid-call signaling, though it was later refined in RFC 6086.

today: RFC 2976 defines the INFO method for mid-session signaling in SIP calls. It was later refined by RFC 6086, but the original method remains in use as the foundation for INFO-based extensions.

sections.title: What INFO Solves
sections.content:
The SIP protocol handles call setup (INVITE), teardown (BYE) and mid-call changes (re-INVITE). However, once a call is established, there is no general way to send session control information along the SIP signaling path. The INFO method fills this gap.

INFO carries application-level information related to the session without changing the call state or session parameters. Examples include DTMF tones during calls, PSTN signaling between gateways, wireless signal strength information, or account balance updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone system can set up calls and hang up calls, but it needs a way to send little messages during the call. INFO is that way.

sections.title: How INFO Works
sections.content:
The INFO method follows the same signaling path that re-INVITE, BYE and other in-session requests use. This path is established during call setup and may involve SIP proxy servers that added themselves to the Record-Route header during the original INVITE.

An INFO request may carry information in message headers or in a message body. A 200 OK response indicates successful delivery. The protocol does not define the format of the body; that is left to extensions using INFO. INFO messages MUST be responded to with a final response (not provisional responses).
sections.plainLanguage: INFO messages travel the same route as the rest of the call. You send one, and the other side sends back a message saying it got it.

sections.title: Header Fields and Message Body
sections.content:
INFO requests support the same header fields as other SIP requests like BYE, with a few specific rules. The Call-ID, CSeq, From, To and Via headers are mandatory. Content-Type and Content-Length headers apply when a message body is present.

The RFC defines rules for handling different response codes: a 200 OK for successful delivery, a 481 Call Leg Does Not Exist if the call is not found, and a 415 Unsupported Media Type if the message body cannot be handled. The CSeq header is incremented for each INFO sent, though the RFC notes that gaps may occur due to re-INVITEs or other messages.
sections.plainLanguage: INFO messages look like other SIP messages but use special rules for what headers must be present and what to do if the message arrives at the wrong call.

sections.title: Restrictions and Guidelines
sections.content:
INFO messages MUST NOT be cancelled with a CANCEL request; instead, the recipient sends a 487 Request Cancelled response if no final response has been sent. An INFO request MUST NOT change the state of the SIP call or the sessions it initiates.

Extensions using INFO should keep message bodies small to avoid fragmentation over UDP. They should be aware that SIP proxy servers may fork INFO messages, and that extending INFO should avoid using the Require or Proxy-Require headers where possible to improve interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: INFO messages are meant to carry extra information, not to break or change the call. Keep them small and simple, and remember that multiple copies might arrive if the network branches them.

sections.title: The INFO Method in Practice
sections.content: The INFO method provides a standard way for mid-session information to travel alongside SIP calls. RFC 2976 defines the mechanism but leaves the body format to extensions. Later, RFC 6086 refined the definition for better interoperability. The original method is still valid and widely used as the basis for INFO-carrying extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: INFO became the standard way for SIP calls to exchange extra messages during the call. Other documents have since clarified how to use it.

references.text: Handley, M., Schulzrinne, H., Schooler, E. and J. Rosenberg, "SIP: Session Initiation Protocol", RFC 2543, March 1999.
